title: Iris and the Grand Oak Hotel
markdown:
The Grand Oak Hotel was old as fallen logs and remembered its seasons the way a desk remembers scratches. Iris the rabbit, whiskers on duty, started her job as bellhop with a notebook of wishes. Mr. Grumbles wanted three juniper berries, counted, not estimated. Miss Pipkin needed silent music, which is a request you honour by walking softly. The butterflies liked their window an inch more open for sunbeams, and an inch was a science.

The Manager, stout, booming, called her aside in the lobby that smelled of oak and polish. “Tonight is the Squirrelly Symphony Ball. Every guest delighted. No slip-ups. The oak remembers slip-ups.” He said it as if the hotel kept minutes.

A flutter arrived in Iris’s chest. Forgetting, on a ball night, would be a career in one word. She whirled anyway: pillows, berries, tiptoe past Miss Pipkin, window for the butterflies. Milo the mole and Mrs. Thread the spider offered quiet nods from their usual corners, which in a hotel counts as a briefing.

By late afternoon she was tired enough to spy a mug and think, just a sip of dandelion tea. The mug was a sleep potion meant for a guest who needed to stay awake. She set it down unsampled. “No shortcuts.” The tea smelled kind. Kind was not the same as permitted.

Then a grand thump-thump: Professor Hoot, who loved stars more than parties, arrived with a list. Perfect silence. No drafts. Telescope just so. The flutter came back and brought friends.

The ball began. Tiny squirrels set up their instruments with the confidence of people who have never been asked to play quietly. A squeaky door let in a draft that ruffled the professor’s star charts. The music found his ears and stayed too long. Iris’s heart sank into her bellhop shoes.

Speed would not fix a draft. Thoughtfulness might. She fetched her softest dandelion-fluff blanket, the one that smelled like a good afternoon, and tucked it behind the squeaky door until the creak became a whisper. Cool air prickled her fur. She tiptoed to the music director. “Professor Hoot is trying to hear the stars. Softer. Like wind through leaves.” The director, who had a career to consider, nodded. The symphony stepped down into a melody that left room for sky.

Professor Hoot felt the quiet and the softer line, peered out, and saw Iris a little chilly without her blanket. He beckoned. “I see the care. Harmony is understanding. Sometimes it is also fluff.” He adjusted the telescope as if fluff were an instrument.

Night settled. Mr. Grumbles had his three berries. Miss Pipkin found a new melody in the hush. The butterflies kept their inch. Professor Hoot charted. Iris felt a warmth that did not come from tea.

She logged berries-three / sleep-mug refused / fluff-at-the-door in the bell book, left the blanket on loan until morning, and let Milo nod once more as if nodding were applause. Mrs. Thread mended a programme with a discreet thread and did not mention the draft again. The Grand Oak hummed. Iris’s ears, which had spent the day twitching, listened instead.
